title: HS Code-Based Industrial Input Declaration and Audit
summary: This thread covers the evolution of documentation requirements for industrial inputs, where HS codes are used to track raw materials, wastage, and production capacity. It evolved from simple declarations to standardized audit reporting formats under the Customs Act 2023.

evolution.procedure: Shifted from manual declaration to systematic audit-based verification and digital inventory tracking.
evolution.institutions: Increased role of the Customs Audit Commissionerate in verifying HS code declarations.

timeline.change: Initial standardized declaration format for footwear production inputs.
Expansion of declaration format to include mould/die production materials.
Integration of HS code usage as a risk factor in transaction-based and system-based audits.
Codification of HS code requirements for bonded warehouse licensing and inventory management.
Refinement of input declaration forms to include total production and usage metrics.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is the issuing authority for the prescribed declaration form required for inputs utilized in footwear manufacturing.
Footwear Manufacturing Inputs: Manufacturers are required to provide a formal declaration detailing the specific inputs used in production, including their respective HS codes, quantities required per unit, and the percentage of wastage for each item.

The declaration must include identification details such as the company name, address, and Value Added Tax registration number, and requires certification by the relevant Value Added Tax Commissioner.

Industrial Mould: This instrument provides a standardized form for declaring raw materials and components used in the production of moulds or dies. It requires applicants to submit specific product details, HS codes, unit measurements, and waste percentages for the materials consumed in the manufacturing process.

The declaration form must be validated with the signature of the applicant's management and countersigned by the relevant Commissioner of Customs or VAT authorities to confirm the input-output coefficients.
Value Added Tax: The document mandates the disclosure of the taxpayer registration number, linking the manufacturing declaration process to the regulatory framework for value-added tax compliance.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is the regulatory authority overseeing the submission and validation of raw material consumption declarations for industrial production.

member_objects.clause_title: ৪.২.১ ট্র্যানজ্যাকশন বেইজড অডিটের জন্য বাছাই কৌশলের নিয়ামকসমূহ

Transaction Based Audit: This standing order provides the criteria and indicators for selecting consignments for transaction-based audits to manage customs risk effectively.
The selection strategy focuses on identifying high-risk transactions based on importer/exporter behavior, transaction values, duty rates, country of origin, and discrepancies in manifest data.
Importer and Exporter: Audit selection criteria consider the frequency and history of importers or exporters.

Operational focus is placed on irregular traders, those frequently providing false declarations, one-time traders, first-time traders, or those importing multiple products under various HS Codes in a single consignment.
H.S. Code: Discrepancies in HS Code usage, such as misclassification of accessories as primary machinery or selecting codes inconsistent with the business nature, are key indicators for audit selection.
Abnormal import volumes under specific codes that do not match market statistics or intentional switching of codes following duty rate changes are flagged as high risk.
Customs Duty: Transactions involving high or low customs duty rates are monitored for risks of revenue leakage or fraudulent classification.
Special attention is required for high-duty items where errors could lead to significant revenue loss, and for zero-rated items susceptible to misclassification to gain improper benefits.
Country of Origin: Misdeclaration of the country of origin is a significant risk factor, particularly for goods subject to quotas or specific import restrictions.
Discrepancies between the declared country of origin and the country of shipment, or importing from restricted sources according to Import Policy Orders, trigger mandatory further verification.
Bill of Lading: The Bill of Lading must be cross-verified against the Import General Manifest to ensure consistency in shipper, consignee, and cargo details.
Declarations of origin and product details in the Bill of Lading are validated as part of the customs audit process to prevent misdeclaration.
Airway Bill: The Airway Bill serves as a critical transport document where declared details such as origin must align with other customs documents to mitigate the risk of fraud.
Import General Manifest: The Import General Manifest submitted by the ship's master or agent is reviewed to compare declarations of product description, value, and quantity against other shipping documents.
Operational checks include verifying the consistency of container details with the provided declarations to ensure accuracy in cargo clearance.

Customs Act 1969: Section 83(C) of the Act serves as the legal basis for issuing official notices to conduct transaction-based audits on imported goods.
Transaction Based Audit: The Audit Team is responsible for conducting a transaction-based audit of specific bills of entry as directed by the Commissioner of Customs.

Auditees are required to present comprehensive documentation regarding their business profile, HS codes, declared values, concessional benefits, and compliance with import policies as part of the audit process.
Commissioner of Customs Valuation and In: This authority or the respective Custom House issues the official notice for the transaction-based audit and oversees the appointment of the audit team.
Import Registration Certificate: Auditees must provide details of their Import Registration Certificate, including its type, to verify their status as industrial or commercial importers.
VAT Compliant: The auditee must submit information confirming their VAT registration status and overall VAT compliance as part of the audit documentation requirements.
H.S. Code: The audit requires verification of declared HS codes against import documents, LCs, and the Bangladesh Customs Tariff, as well as checking against any advance rulings provided by the National Board of Revenue.
National Board of Revenue: The board is responsible for issuing advance rulings on HS codes and granting special concessions or privileges that are subject to review during a customs audit.
Customs Procedure Code: The audit examines concessional benefits claimed under various SROs or special orders to ensure that the appropriate Customs Procedure Code conditions have been satisfied, such as the installation of imported capital machinery.

Transaction Based Audit: This clause provides a comprehensive standard template and guidelines for conducting transaction-based audits of business entities. It outlines required documentation, verification procedures for classification and valuation, and instructions for assessing compliance with import policies and customs duty concessions.
Auditors are instructed to use a risk management approach to randomly sample documents when the volume of bills of entry or other import records is extensive.
H.S. Code: Auditors must verify whether declared HS Codes align with import documents, bills of entry, and letters of credit while ensuring conformity with the Bangladesh Customs Tariff and WCO Explanatory Notes.
Verification includes assessing the application of NBR advance rulings, laboratory reports, and checking for potential misclassification intended to avoid higher duties or import bans.
Exchange Rate: Auditors are required to verify that the correct exchange rates have been applied to imported goods during the assessment process.
Identical Goods: During valuation audits, officers must compare the declared value of imported goods against the value of identical or similar goods imported around the same time to ensure accuracy.
Customs Procedure Code: The audit must verify if goods imported under specific concessional facilities or customs procedure codes comply with all conditions stipulated in the relevant SROs or government orders.
It includes checking if capital machinery imported at a concessional rate is properly installed and if input quantities align with registered production coefficients.
VAT Compliant: Business entities subject to customs audits must be evaluated on whether they maintain VAT compliant status as part of their organizational profile.
Risk Management: When processing large volumes of import documentation, auditors are directed to perform audits based on risk management principles, which involve randomly selecting samples for verification.

System Based Audit: This standing order provides a comprehensive structured checklist for conducting system-based audits of business entities under customs supervision.

Auditors are instructed to evaluate enterprise resource planning data, import-export documentation, valuation compliance, and adherence to specific regulatory rules to identify irregularities or duty evasion.
Authorized Economic Operator: The audit framework requires verification of whether a business entity is registered as an Authorized Economic Operator.
H.S. Code: Auditors must verify that declared HS Codes are consistent with import documents, LCs, BCT, and WCO explanatory notes, and check for misuse of preferential or zero-duty codes.
Risk Management: When dealing with large volumes of bills of entry or documentation, auditors should apply risk management principles to select samples for audit verification.
VAT Compliant: The audit process must confirm the VAT compliant status of the subject entity as part of its operational documentation review.
Manufacturing Process: Auditors are required to verify the manufacturing process, bill of materials, and production flow when examining the ERP or internal software systems of the entity.
London Metal Exchange: Price verification for metal imports should include cross-referencing against data from the London Metal Exchange.
Platts: Auditors should use data from Platts to verify the declared value of energy, petrochemicals, and metal commodities.
Customs: The document serves as a standardized audit reporting template for customs officers to evaluate business records and identify potential customs duty evasion or regulatory non-compliance.
Materials: Verification procedures include examining the input-output coefficients and raw material usage to ensure compliance with bonded warehouse and duty exemption requirements.
Service: The audit must cover valuation of services such as royalty, transportation, and technical fees to ensure they are accurately declared and accounted for in the customs value.
Lock: The audit requires verification of any history of BIN surveillance or locks, including the reasons for such actions and any associated penalties.

Customs Act 1969: This standing order provides a standardized template for a show-cause notice issued under Section 32(2) of the Act to determine duties and taxes under Section 32(4) in cases of misdeclaration of imported goods.
It identifies misdeclaration of HS codes as a punishable offence under Section 32(1) and specifies that penalties apply according to Clause 14 of Table-1 under Section 156 of the Act.

The document outlines the procedure for recovery of short-paid duties and grants the customs authority power to finalize assessments based on available documentation if a response is not received within the specified timeframe.
Bangladesh Customs Tariff: The tariff is cited as a key reference document, alongside legal instruments and international explanatory notes, used by the customs authority during post-clearance audits to verify the accuracy of declarations.
World Customs Organization: The organization's explanatory notes are utilized as a standard reference for the classification and assessment of imported goods during post-clearance audit procedures.
Customs Clearance: The procedure includes a requirement for the C&F agent to submit a bill of entry for the clearance of goods, which is subsequently subject to review during post-clearance audits.

Bonded Warehouse License: To obtain a license, a person must submit an application in the prescribed form along with verified supporting documents, court fees, and other mandatory certificates. The application process requires the fulfillment of specific criteria such as facility size, operational history, and financial stability, as well as adherence to safety and legal standards. All accompanying documentation, including business registration and utility records, must be verified by the lien bank to ensure authenticity.
Value Added Tax: A valid Value Added Tax registration certificate is a mandatory requirement for applying for a bonded warehouse license.
Business Registration: Applicants must submit various registration documents, including trade licenses, fire licenses, and registration certificates from regulatory bodies like BoI or BSCIC, as part of the licensing process.
Industrial Raw Materials: The license application requires detailed documentation regarding raw materials, including commercial descriptions and HS codes, and mandates that storage facilities for these materials meet international quality standards.
Bonded Warehouse Operation: The operation of a bonded warehouse requires an applicant to demonstrate that the facility is physically secure with defined boundaries and adequate storage capacity. Licensees are required to comply with all domestic laws and regulations, providing a notarized affidavit as a formal commitment to this compliance.

(৩) যুগপৎ সরাসরি ও প্রচ্ছন্ন রপ্তানিকারক হিসেবে নতুন ওয়্যারহাউস লাইসেন্সের আবেদনের ক্ষেত্রে লাইসেন্সিং বিধিমালায় নির্দেশিত দলিলাদির অতিরিক্ত হিসেবে বিনিয়োগ বোর্ড ও সংশ্লিষ্ট অনুমোদিত অ্যাসোসিয়েশন (প্রযোজ্য ক্ষেত্রে) এর সুপারিশে “সরাসরি ও প্রচ্ছন্ন রপ্তানিকারক” প্রতিষ্ঠান মর্মে উল্লেখ থাকিতে হইবে।
(৪) বিদ্যমান ওয়্যারহাউস লাইসেন্সে সরাসরি রপ্তানিকারকের পাশাপাশি প্রচ্ছন্ন রপ্তানিকারক কিংবা প্রচ্ছন্ন রপ্তানিকারক এর পাশাপাশি সরাসরি রপ্তানিকারকের সংযোজন করিয়া ওয়্যারহাউস লাইসেন্সের পরিস্থিতি পরিবর্তনের ক্ষেত্রে সংশ্লিষ্ট অ্যাসোসিয়েশনের সুপারিশ এবং বিনিয়োগ বোর্ড হইতে সংশোধনী গ্রহণ করিয়া লাইসেন্সিং কর্তৃপক্ষ বরাবর আবেদন দাখিল করিতে হইবে।

(৯) সরাসরি রপ্তানির ক্ষেত্রে রপ্তানি ঋণপত্র, সেলস্ কন্ট্র্যাক্ট ও ইউডি এর ভিত্তিতে উপকরণ আমদানি করা হইলে তাহা পাশবইয়ে এবং বন্ড রেজিস্টারে এন্ট্রি করিতে হইবে এবং ইউপির বিপরীতে উপকরণের ব্যবহার নিশ্চিত করিয়া বন্ড রেজিস্টার ও পাশবইয়ে এন্ট্রি করিয়া এক্সবন্ডের মাধ্যমে রপ্তানি নিশ্চিত করিতে হইবে।

Bonded Warehouse: Industrial enterprises are permitted to hold a license to operate simultaneously as both direct and deemed exporters.
Existing warehouse license holders may apply to change their status to operate as both direct and deemed exporters with the approval of the licensing authority.

All imported or collected raw materials must be entered into the bonded warehouse under the supervision of a bond officer and recorded in the bond register upon usage against a utilization declaration.
Bonded Warehouse License: Applications for new licenses involving both direct and deemed exports require specific recommendations from the investment board and relevant associations.

To modify an existing license to include additional export categories, enterprises must obtain recommendations from relevant associations and approval from the investment board before applying to the licensing authority.
The license must be updated to include the details and HS codes of all materials and finished goods used in both direct and deemed export operations as recommended by the investment board.
Annual Import Entitlement: For industries other than garment manufacturing, the annual import entitlement is determined based on the production capacity of declared machinery and in accordance with the relevant rules and consumption coefficients approved by the department.
Utilization Declaration: Issuance of a utilization declaration is mandatory for both direct and deemed exports.
For deemed exports, a utilization declaration cannot be issued without the consumption coefficient approved by the department.
Direct Export Procedures: When importing materials for direct export based on export letters of credit, sales contracts, and utilization declarations, the materials must be recorded in the passbook and bond register.

Exporters must ensure the utilization of imported materials against the utilization declaration, record the usage in the bond register and passbook, and complete the ex-bonding process to finalize the export.

Bonded Warehouse Operation: Raw materials and auxiliary items, including their HS codes, approved within the license or supplementary Utilization Declaration, may be imported duty-free under the bonded warehouse system.

Industrial entities may import raw materials outside of their standard license scope subject to certification by the Commissioner of Customs Bond or another authorized customs official for valid reasons.
Back-to-Back Letter of Credit: Industrial entities are permitted to import raw materials against a confirmed sales contract or an export master letter of credit through the opening of back-to-back letters of credit.
The total value of all back-to-back letters of credit issued against such export contracts must not exceed the limits prescribed by the prevailing Import Policy Order.
Free of Cost (FOC) Import: Industrial entities may import raw materials on a Free of Cost basis, provided the quantity does not exceed one-third of the products exported in the preceding audit period and the entity's lien bank provides a no-objection certificate.

For industries receiving over 80 percent of raw materials as Free of Cost from foreign buyers and earning only Cutting, Making and Trimming charges, imports are permitted on a revolving basis for up to six months subject to specific approval and performance documentation.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs Bond, or an authorized alternate, is responsible for approving the importation of non-licensed raw materials, verifying export performance, and monitoring the revolving import allowance for entities operating under the Cutting, Making and Trimming model.
